name: B2B SaaS Fundraising Pitch Deck
description: A dark, investor-ready B2B SaaS fundraising deck in black navy, momentum green, and evidence blue for defining an urgent enterprise problem, explaining an end-to-end product workflow, sizing the reachable market, proving commercial validation, and connecting the financing ask to milestones.
style_guide:
# Dark SaaS Fundraising

## Design intent

Create a rigorous, investor-ready B2B SaaS deck on a near-black navy canvas. The presentation should feel commercially mature, concise, and operationally credible rather than futuristic. Use deep navy panels to organize evidence, emerald to signal momentum and the preferred path, blue to distinguish supporting proof or a second category, amber for bounded opportunity, and red only for genuine pain or downside.

Every page must make one decision-relevant claim, support it with a small number of inspectable modules, and make the implication obvious. Preserve the visual grammar shown by the previews, but do not copy their company, industry, facts, numbers, dates, labels, or slide sequence. The preview images are UI-only references; this written guide is the complete authoring authority.

## Non-negotiable page grammar

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64–68 px` left and right safe margins and a `36–44 px` footer zone. No essential content may touch the canvas edge.
- Use a 12-column grid with `20–28 px` gutters. Align titles, panel edges, card tops, values, dividers, and footer marks to shared grid lines.
- Content pages start with a short `3–4 px` emerald vertical rule at the upper-left of the title block. Place the title and subtitle `16–20 px` to its right.
- Reserve roughly `94–112 px` for the title region, followed by `30–40 px` of breathing room before the main analytical structure.
- Use `20–28 px` gaps between major panels and `14–20 px` gaps within a panel. Prefer two to four strong modules over many dashboard tiles.
- Add a thin footer rule, a quiet deck or company label at bottom-left, and a current-page/total-page indicator at bottom-right.
- The cover is the deliberate exception to the content-page header: it uses a long emerald vertical anchor, a spacious left-aligned title block, and a lower metadata row.

## Color system

### Surfaces and text

- Canvas black-navy: `#070B19`. Use as the full-slide background.
- Primary panel navy: `#0F162E`. Use for large analytical containers and grouped modules.
- Elevated card navy: `#162044`. Use for proof rows, founder cards, selected tiers, KPI modules, and active evidence.
- Deep inset navy: `#0B1124`. Use for a lower visual level such as an unselected tier, chart well, or nested detail.
- Structural stroke: `#1A2444`. Use for one-pixel borders, separators, footer rules, and inactive rails.
- Primary white: `#F8FAFC`. Use for titles, claims, values, panel headings, and critical labels.
- Secondary slate: `#94A3B8`. Use for subtitles, body copy, axes, and explanations.
- Quiet slate: `#64748B`. Use for metadata, sources, inactive milestones, and page numbers.

### Semantic accents

- Momentum emerald: `#10B981`. This is the identity color. Use for header rules, active borders, bullets, progress, primary actions, and positive commercial signals.
- Outcome mint: `#34D399`. Use for the strongest positive number, funding value, active milestone, or final outcome.
- Evidence blue: `#3B82F6`. Use for validation, a comparison entity, expansion, or the second process stage.
- Evidence blue text: `#93C5FD`. Use only for short blue-coded labels or supporting phrases.
- Opportunity amber: `#F59E0B`. Use for a reachable market, conversion evidence, or a third allocation category.
- Risk red: `#EF4444`. Reserve for sourced loss, failure, critical pain, or downside.

### Color discipline

- Keep at least 70 percent of each page in the black-navy and panel-navy family. Concentrate saturated accents in rules, dots, borders, values, connectors, and short phrases rather than large fills.
- Emerald remains dominant across the deck; blue supports it. Amber and red are semantic exceptions, not decoration.
- Use no more than three saturated accents on an ordinary page. A chart may use more only when categories require them and every category is labeled.
- Never rely on color alone. Pair it with a label, number, position, icon, line treatment, or direct annotation.
- Use flat fills. Do not introduce gradients, glow, glass effects, or luminous borders.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter` when available, otherwise `Arial` or a compatible system sans-serif. For CJK output, use a common system CJK sans-serif with comparable weight and width.
- Use scale and weight for hierarchy; do not use decorative display faces.
- Cover eyebrow: `13–15 px`, weight `700`, uppercase when the language supports it, letter-spacing `2–3 px`, Momentum emerald.
- Cover title: `50–60 px`, weight `800–900`, line-height `1.02–1.08`, Primary white. Prefer two balanced lines.
- Cover subtitle: `20–23 px`, weight `400`, line-height `1.35–1.45`, Secondary slate.
- Content-page title: `30–36 px`, weight `800`, line-height `1.08–1.15`, Primary white. Make it a conclusion rather than a topic label.
- Content-page subtitle: `16–18 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.35–1.45`, Secondary slate.
- Major panel title: `19–22 px`, weight `700–800`; card title: `16–18 px`, weight `700–800`.
- Body copy and bullets: `13–15 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.45–1.6`, Secondary slate.
- Hero metric or funding value: `34–48 px`, weight `800–900`; ordinary KPI value: `24–32 px`, weight `800`.
- Pills, legends, timeline labels, and table headers: `10–12 px`, weight `600–700`. Sources and footer text: `9–11 px`, Quiet slate.
- Do not force an extra module by shrinking essential copy. Keep paragraphs to two to four lines and split longer reasoning into bullets.

## Components and hierarchy

- Major panels use Primary panel navy, a `1 px` Structural stroke border, `8–10 px` corner radius, and no shadow.
- Nested cards use Elevated card navy. Use Deep inset navy for deliberately secondary or unselected content.
- A selected or recommended card may use a `2 px` emerald or blue edge. Do not fill the whole card with a saturated color.
- Pills use dark or transparent fills, a one-pixel semantic border, `14–18 px` radius, and a short label.
- Section dots are `7–9 px` circles. Use emerald by default and another accent only when that module has a different semantic role.
- A strong bottom summary band may state the implication, problem impact, value proposition, or investment takeaway. It must remain shorter and visually quieter than the page title.
- Within every module, order information as: category label, decisive value or statement, supporting evidence, then implication.
- Use one dominant structure per page: claim ribbon, card trio, process flow, market hierarchy, pricing comparison, milestone timeline, or funding block. Avoid competing hero regions.

## Data, charts, and diagrams

- Prefer business-native visuals: milestone timelines, three-stage flows, market-size stacks, pricing comparisons, allocation lists, simple funnels, grouped bars, horizontal progress bars, and one- or two-series trends.
- Use emerald for the primary trajectory or desired state, blue for proof or the next phase, amber for reachable opportunity, and red for downside.
- Chart wells use Primary panel navy or Deep inset navy. Grid lines and inactive rails use Structural stroke.
- Label decisive values directly and remove legends when direct labels are clearer. Every factual number needs a unit, period, and source or evidence context when applicable.
- Distinguish actuals, assumptions, targets, and forecasts with explicit text and line treatment. Never invent market size, pricing, customer, traction, ROI, runway, or fundraising figures to complete a composition.
- Timelines use a thin rail, small circular markers, a compact period label, a bold outcome, and one short explanation. Use emerald for current or achieved, blue for next, and Quiet slate for later.
- Process flows use three or four equal stage cards and thin directional connectors. Keep the final commercial outcome in a separate summary band.
- Allocation lists pair a colored dot and label on the left with a bold percentage on the right; when percentages represent a whole, they must sum correctly.

## Adaptable composition families

These are composition tendencies, not executable templates, fixed slide requirements, or permission to reuse preview content. Select the family that best serves the current Outline Entry.

- Cover: use an asymmetric left-aligned composition with a long emerald anchor, small fundraising-stage eyebrow, large two-line thesis, restrained subtitle, one or two outlined thesis pills, and presenter/company/date metadata along the lower grid. Preserve generous empty space.
- Problem or risk: use three equal evidence cards with a semantic dot, concise heading, one sourced impact statement when available, and no more than three bullets. Close with one full-width impact band.
- Solution or product: use three equal stages linked by simple arrows, such as input, orchestration, and insight when those concepts fit. Close with a full-width value proposition and one grounded outcome.
- Customer and market: use a balanced 6/6 split. Define ICP, buyer, and deployment context on one side; show TAM/SAM/SOM or another opportunity hierarchy as stacked modules on the other.
- Commercial model and validation: use two large panels. Compare no more than three pricing or packaging tiers on one side and stack two or three proof rows on the other. Highlight only one recommended option.
- Team, milestones, and funding: place a full-width milestone timeline above two lower panels. Use compact leadership cards on the left and make the funding target the strongest value on the right.
- Traction or financial outlook: use one dominant chart plus two or three supporting KPIs or a narrow proof rail. Clearly label actuals and forecasts.
- Competition: use one restrained matrix, capability comparison, or position map, plus a concise implication module. Keep competitor colors quiet so the company's emerald signal remains dominant.
- Closing or ask: return to a sparse composition with the investable thesis, ask, use of funds, next milestone, and one explicit call to action.

## Core solution workflow page

- Explain the product through three connected operational stages rather than an undifferentiated feature inventory. Use stage names that describe the real workflow, such as ingest, orchestrate, decide, act, reconcile, or report.
- Each stage needs an input, transformation or action, output, user or system owner, and one proof point. Do not claim automation, real-time operation, accuracy, cycle-time reduction, or error reduction unless the workspace supports it.
- Keep three stage cards equal in width and connect them with thin directional arrows. A blue-coded middle stage may show coordination or orchestration; emerald should identify the primary value path and final outcome.
- Close the page with a full-width value proposition band that translates workflow capability into buyer outcomes. If ROI is available, show calculation basis, period, denominator, included costs, and whether the value is observed, customer-reported, modeled, or targeted.
- Separate product capability, integration dependency, implementation service, customer process change, and resulting business outcome. A workflow diagram must not imply that an unbuilt integration or unsupported action already exists.
- Treat preview workflow names, feature claims, performance improvements, and ROI as fictional visual reference content. Rebuild the entire product story from the current workspace.

## Imagery and allowed variation

- The default language is typographic and data-led. Photography is optional. Prefer readable product interface crops, workflow diagrams, customer environments, or relevant industry evidence inside aligned rectangles.
- Use one minimal line or solid icon family at `16–24 px`. Icons are labels, not hero decoration. Avoid generic handshake, rocket, glowing server, city-at-night, robot, or abstract AI imagery.
- Preserve the canvas, title anchor, typography hierarchy, panel construction, footer, and semantic colors while varying composition according to the message.
- Pages may be sparse or information-rich, symmetric or asymmetric. Every page still needs one dominant claim and an obvious reading path.
- Adapt line length, tracking, and wrapping to the confirmed output language. Do not force English capitalization conventions onto other scripts.

## Avoid

- Do not reproduce names, metrics, dates, market values, pricing, founder histories, customer claims, or fundraising terms from preview images unless grounded in the current Workspace.
- Do not turn the style into a generic neon technology deck. Avoid glow, circuit-board decoration, sci-fi motifs, and excessive cyan.
- Do not use light slide backgrounds, white cards, pastel palettes, photographic wallpapers, heavy shadows, glass effects, 3D charts, or oversized radii.
- Do not use emerald, blue, amber, and red interchangeably. Preserve their semantic roles.
- Do not use tiny dashboard tiles, dense tables, more than four major panels, long paragraphs, or centered content-page copy.
- Do not repeat the same three-card layout on every page. Reuse the visual grammar while choosing a structure appropriate to the investor question.
